about: Sourced life stories for Rome: the emperors Scripture names (Augustus, Tiberius, Claudius), Nero by date only, and the seven officials before whom Jesus and Paul were heard or who are named beside them. Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossier Research/People/rulers-rome.md.

augustus-luk-2-1.short: The emperor whose decree that all the world should be taxed took Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, where Jesus was born.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Caesar Augustus once, at the opening of Luke's account of Jesus' birth: "there went out a decree from Cæsar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." Luke dates the taxing by a governor: it "was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria".

"And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city." Joseph went up from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem in Judaea, "the city of David", because he was of the house and lineage of David. He went to be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, who was great with child. While they were there she brought forth her firstborn son and laid him in a manger, "because there was no room for them in the inn."

That is all Scripture tells of him. It does not say what the taxing was for, or whether the whole world was enrolled at one time, and it records no other act of his. In Acts the word comes again: Festus speaks of Paul's appeal "unto the hearing of Augustus", and Paul sails in the care of "a centurion of Augustus' band". The site does not count those verses as this man's; his page as a ruler explains how they use the word.

quirinius-luk-2-2.short: Governor of Syria, named once by Luke to date the taxing that took Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem; Scripture says nothing else of him.

paragraphs.text: Luke names him in a single verse, set in brackets: "(And this taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria.)" Cyrenius is the name in the King James text; the site calls him Quirinius and explains the name on his page as a ruler. The taxing was the one decreed by Caesar Augustus, under which Joseph went up from Nazareth to Bethlehem with Mary.

That is all Scripture says of him. It records no word or act of his and does not say whether he came to Judaea himself. In Acts, Gamaliel recalls "Judas of Galilee in the days of the taxing", who "drew away much people after him" and "also perished"; he names no governor. How Luke's date fits what is known from outside the Bible is set out, as views with their holders, on his page as a ruler.

tiberius-mat-22-17.short: The emperor by whose fifteenth year Luke dates the coming of the word of God to John the Baptist; Scripture names him only there.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Tiberius once. Luke dates the start of John's preaching by him: "Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Cæsar ... the word of God came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness." John then came into all the country about Jordan, "preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins".

In the same verse Luke names the rulers of that year: Pontius Pilate governor of Judaea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, with Annas and Caiaphas as the high priests. Scripture gives no length for his reign and says nothing of his death or of who came after him.

Elsewhere in the Gospels the emperor is only "Caesar". In Matthew, Jesus was asked, "Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not?" He called for the tribute money, was brought a penny, and asked whose image and superscription it bore. When they said Caesar's, he answered, "Render therefore unto Cæsar the things which are Cæsar's; and unto God the things that are God's." Mark and Luke tell the same exchange in their own words.

At the trial before Pilate, Luke says the accusers charged Jesus with "forbidding to give tribute to Cæsar". John says the Jews cried, "If thou let this man go, thou art not Cæsar's friend", and the chief priests said, "We have no king but Cæsar." None of these verses, and none of the tribute verses, names the emperor. The site's person record files them under Tiberius, and his page as a ruler explains why.

pilate-mat-27-2.short: The governor of Judaea who questioned Jesus, said he found no fault in him, released Barabbas, and delivered Jesus to be crucified.

paragraphs.text: Luke names "Pontius Pilate being governor of Judæa" in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, and Matthew calls him "Pontius Pilate the governor". Luke alone tells that some told Jesus "of the Galilæans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices"; he does not say when or why. Scripture does not name Pilate's wife or tell how his governorship ended.

Matthew and Mark tell that in the morning the chief priests bound Jesus and delivered him to Pilate; John says they would not go into the judgment hall themselves, "lest they should be defiled". Luke gives their charge: "perverting the nation, and forbidding to give tribute to Cæsar, saying that he himself is Christ a King." All four Gospels have Pilate ask, "Art thou the King of the Jews?" In Matthew, Mark and Luke, Jesus answers "Thou sayest" (in Mark and Luke, "Thou sayest it"); in Matthew and Mark he then answered his accusers nothing, and Pilate marvelled.

John alone tells a longer exchange inside the judgment hall. Jesus said, "My kingdom is not of this world"; Pilate asked, "What is truth?", went out, and told the Jews, "I find in him no fault at all." Later, when the Jews said Jesus "made himself the Son of God", Pilate "was the more afraid" and asked him, "Whence art thou?", and Jesus gave him no answer. When Pilate spoke of his power to crucify him or release him, Jesus answered, "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above".

Luke alone tells that Pilate, learning that Jesus belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, sent him to Herod, who was in Jerusalem; Herod mocked him and sent him back. "The same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together: for before they were at enmity between themselves." In Luke, Pilate says three times that he found no fault or "no cause of death" in him, and offers to chastise him and let him go: "I will therefore chastise him, and release him." In John, too, Pilate says three times that he found no fault in him.

All four Gospels tell of releasing a prisoner at the feast, and that the crowd asked for Barabbas rather than Jesus. Matthew says the chief priests and elders "persuaded the multitude", and Mark that the chief priests "moved the people"; both say Pilate knew Jesus had been delivered "for envy". Matthew alone tells that as Pilate sat on the judgment seat his wife sent him word: "Have thou nothing to do with that just man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him." Matthew alone tells that Pilate "took water, and washed his hands before the multitude", saying, "I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it", and that the people answered, "His blood be on us, and on our children."

Matthew says Pilate released Barabbas, "and when he had scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified"; Mark tells the same, and says Pilate did it "willing to content the people". In John, Pilate scourged Jesus before the sentence: the soldiers put a crown of thorns and a purple robe on Jesus, and Pilate brought him out and said, "Behold the man!" When the Jews cried, "If thou let this man go, thou art not Cæsar's friend", Pilate sat down in the judgment seat at the Pavement, "in the Hebrew, Gabbatha", and delivered him to be crucified. Luke says "Pilate gave sentence that it should be as they required" and "delivered Jesus to their will." Mark sets the crucifixion at "the third hour"; John has Pilate at Gabbatha "about the sixth hour".

Matthew, Mark and Luke each give the written accusation over the cross in their own words, and Luke says it was written in Greek, Latin and Hebrew. John says Pilate wrote the title, "JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS", in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, and when the chief priests asked him to change it he answered, "What I have written I have written." All four Gospels tell that Joseph of Arimathaea asked Pilate for the body of Jesus. Matthew, Mark and John say Pilate granted it, and Mark alone tells that "Pilate marvelled if he were already dead" and asked the centurion first. Matthew alone tells that the chief priests and Pharisees asked him to make the tomb sure, and Pilate said, "Ye have a watch: go your way, make it as sure as ye can."

Pilate is named again after the Gospels. Peter told the men of Israel that they had denied Jesus "in the presence of Pilate, when he was determined to let him go." Peter and John's company said in prayer that "both Herod, and Pontius Pilate" had been gathered together "against thy holy child Jesus", and Paul preached at Antioch in Pisidia that though they found no cause of death in him, "yet desired they Pilate that he should be slain." First Timothy speaks of Christ Jesus, "who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession".

lysanias-luk-3-1.short: Tetrarch of Abilene, named once in Luke's list of rulers for the year the word of God came to John; Scripture says nothing more.

paragraphs.text: Lysanias is named in a single verse. Luke dates the coming of the word of God to John in the wilderness by the rulers of that year, and ends the list with "Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene".

Scripture records no word or deed of his, and does not say whose son he was or how long he ruled. Which Lysanias Luke means, and what is known of rulers of that name from outside the Bible, are set out on his page as a ruler.

claudius-act-11-28.short: The emperor in whose days the famine Agabus foretold came to pass, and who commanded all Jews to depart from Rome.

paragraphs.text: Acts names the emperor Claudius twice. At Antioch a prophet from Jerusalem named Agabus "signified by the Spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Cæsar." The disciples, "every man according to his ability", sent relief to the brethren in Judaea by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

At Corinth Paul found a Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, "lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla", "because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome". Paul stayed with them and worked with them, for they were tentmakers. Acts does not say why Claudius gave the command.

Elsewhere Acts says only "Caesar". At Thessalonica, Jason and certain brethren were drawn before the rulers of the city, accused of doing "contrary to the decrees of Cæsar"; the verse names no emperor, and the site lists it under Claudius because it falls in his time. The Caesar to whom Paul later appealed the site places in Nero's time instead; his page as a ruler explains why. Scripture says nothing of Claudius's death or of who came after him.

sergius-paulus-act-13-7.short: The deputy of Cyprus at Paphos, a prudent man who sent for Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God, and believed.

paragraphs.text: When Barnabas and Saul had gone through the isle of Cyprus to Paphos, they found a sorcerer, a Jew named Bar-jesus, "Which was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man". The deputy "called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God." "Deputy" is the King James word for his office; his page as a ruler explains the title.

Elymas the sorcerer withstood them, "seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith". Saul, "filled with the Holy Ghost", set his eyes on him and told him that the hand of the Lord was upon him and he would be blind for a season. "And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness".

"Then the deputy, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord." Acts says nothing more of him. It does not say that he was baptized, and it tells nothing of him after Paul and his company sailed from Paphos to Perga.

gallio-act-18-12.short: The deputy of Achaia who would not judge the Jews' charge against Paul at Corinth and drove them from the judgment seat.

paragraphs.text: Paul stayed at Corinth a year and six months, teaching the word of God. "When Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat", saying, "This fellow persuadeth men to worship God contrary to the law."

Before Paul could open his mouth, Gallio answered the Jews. If it were "a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness", he would bear with them: "But if it be a question of words and names, and of your law, look ye to it; for I will be no judge of such matters." "And he drave them from the judgment seat."

Then "all the Greeks took Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. And Gallio cared for none of those things." Paul stayed on at Corinth "yet a good while" and then sailed for Syria. Acts does not say how long Gallio held office or what became of him; what is known of him from outside the Bible is on his page as a ruler.

felix-act-23-24.short: The governor at Caesarea who heard Paul's case, listened to him with his wife Drusilla and trembled, kept him two years, and left him bound when Festus came.

paragraphs.text: When the Jews laid wait for Paul in Jerusalem, the chief captain sent him by night under guard to Caesarea, to "Felix the governor", with a letter: "Claudius Lysias unto the most excellent governor Felix sendeth greeting." The letter said Paul was accused "of questions of their law", but had nothing laid to his charge "worthy of death or of bonds". Felix read it and asked what province Paul was from. Hearing Cilicia, he said he would hear him when his accusers came, and had him kept "in Herod's judgment hall".

Five days later Ananias the high priest came down with the elders and an orator named Tertullus. Tertullus began by praising Felix, "Seeing that by thee we enjoy great quietness", and called Paul "a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition" and "a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes". Paul answered, "Forasmuch as I know that thou hast been of many years a judge unto this nation, I do the more cheerfully answer for myself", and denied the charges.

Felix, "having more perfect knowledge of that way", put them off until Lysias the chief captain should come, and had a centurion keep Paul but let his friends come to him. After certain days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, "which was a Jewess", sent for Paul, and heard him "concerning the faith in Christ". "And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled", and said, "Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee."

Felix "hoped also that money should have been given him of Paul, that he might loose him", so he sent for him often and talked with him. "But after two years Porcius Festus came into Felix' room: and Felix, willing to shew the Jews a pleasure, left Paul bound." Acts does not say whether Paul gave him anything, what Felix came to believe, or what became of him. Drusilla is named only once; what is known of her family from outside the Bible is set out on Felix's page as a ruler.

nero-php-4-22.short: Scripture never names Nero; the site attaches to him, by date, the Caesar to whom Paul appealed, as his page as a ruler explains.

paragraphs.text: Scripture never names Nero. The site places him by date: the "Caesar" to whom Paul appealed before the governor Festus is taken to be Nero, for reasons given, with their sources, on his page as a ruler. The site's person record is built on the greeting in Philippians from "they that are of Caesar's household", a verse that also says only "Caesar".

At Caesarea, when Festus asked Paul whether he would go up to Jerusalem to be judged, Paul answered, "I stand at Cæsar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged", and "I appeal unto Cæsar." Festus answered, "unto Cæsar shalt thou go." Festus called it an appeal "unto the hearing of Augustus" and said he had "no certain thing to write unto my lord". After hearing Paul, king Agrippa said, "This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Cæsar."

Paul was sent to Italy in the care of Julius, "a centurion of Augustus' band". In the storm at sea the angel of God stood by him and said, "Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Cæsar". At Rome Paul told the chief of the Jews that he was "constrained to appeal unto Cæsar; not that I had ought to accuse my nation of."

Acts ends without telling whether the appeal was heard, or by whom. At Rome Paul lived "with a soldier that kept him", and "dwelt two whole years in his own hired house", preaching "no man forbidding him". Writing to the saints at Philippi, Paul said his bonds in Christ were "manifest in all the palace", and closed, "All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household." Who that household was is not said; the views are on Nero's page as a ruler.

festus-act-24-27.short: The governor who followed Felix, heard Paul at Caesarea, granted his appeal to Caesar, and laid his case before king Agrippa.

paragraphs.text: Porcius Festus came "into Felix' room" after Paul had been held two years. Three days after he came into the province he went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem, where the high priest and the chief of the Jews asked him to send for Paul, "laying wait in the way to kill him". Festus answered that Paul would be kept at Caesarea, and told those able among them to come down and accuse him there.

At Caesarea he sat on the judgment seat, and the Jews laid "many and grievous complaints against Paul, which they could not prove." Festus, "willing to do the Jews a pleasure", asked Paul, "Wilt thou go up to Jerusalem, and there be judged of these things before me?" Paul answered, "I stand at Cæsar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged", and "I appeal unto Cæsar." When he had conferred with the council, Festus said, "Hast thou appealed unto Cæsar? unto Cæsar shalt thou go."

When king Agrippa and Bernice came to salute him, Festus laid Paul's cause before the king. He said, "It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face". The accusers, he said, had brought questions "of their own superstition, and of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive." Paul had appealed "unto the hearing of Augustus", and Festus was keeping him until he could send him to Caesar.

The next day, before Agrippa, Bernice and the principal men of the city, Festus said he had found that Paul "had committed nothing worthy of death", yet he had "no certain thing to write unto my lord", and so had brought him before the king. As Paul spoke, Festus said with a loud voice, "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad." Paul answered, "I am not mad, most noble Festus". Afterwards the king, the governor, Bernice and those with them said among themselves, "This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds", and Agrippa told Festus that Paul "might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Cæsar."

"And when it was determined that we should sail into Italy", Paul and other prisoners were handed to Julius, "a centurion of Augustus' band". Acts does not give what Festus wrote to Caesar about Paul, and does not say how long Festus governed or how he died.
